commenti.body:
I love what Fassbinder said about it:

“Robert Bresson’s _The Devil, Probably_ is the most shattering film I’ve seen this Berlin Festival. I think it’s a major film. In the future—and this world will probably last for another few thousand years — this film will be more important than all the rubbish which is now considered important but which never really goes deep enough. The questions Bresson asks will never be unimportant.”
Yeah Bresson is probably the most fascinating director I've come across. How do you feel about my interpretation?

For me this is just another deeply Dostoevskian work by Bresson who is one of the GOATs of cinema and one of my personal favorite directors. I think Charles is ambivalent. That’s the point of the film. He has seemingly everything to live for in his youth and passion, but his clarity on how fucked up the world adults have left for him is and his current mood collides in tragedy. He maybe wouldn’t have chosen to die right when he did at the moment it happens, but his being hopeless and suicidal over the state of the world isn’t presented as unreasonable or unsympathetic. Given what we see of the world as we watch the film it seems like an entirely rational decision to opt out of it all.

Interesting me personally I've always found hope and beauty In everything and I think Bresson did too in his own way. Charles himself seems a little selfish and short sighted while Micheal never stops having hope in that the world will change for the better. If the world was as bleak in this movie that people say it is I dont think Bresson would add a character like Micheal or even the the old lady in l,argent who loves everyone unconditionally so when Yvon kills her he realizes just how far gone he's become and turns himself in for the better. There's always beauty and hope to be found in these films imo.

The film is nihilistic or hopeless, nor is the act of making it. But the reason it’s so powerful is that Bresson presents the case for hopelessness from the POV of someone like Charles with such thoroughness and lack of judgement. This isn’t an afterschool special and it’s not even “It’s a Wonderful Life” (a film I also love and do not mean to knock by comparison)
Yeah I'm done with a Bresson film it leaves me with a blank feeling because it feels like real life almost not a story. Its alot of things.

Another Fassbinder quote:

  
"*The Devil, Probably* is certainly the film of an old man, but no one can deny that the film is incredibly young in spirit -- whether it's an acceptance of suicide or a glorification of it, or, as I think, the opposite, that is, as Bresson says: You have more opportunities to live your life if you accept death. It's simply incredibly beautiful, even just from the point of view of form, when you see someone who's so old, and had already reached an end with *Lancelot*, didn't simply turn out an old man's film with *The Devil, Probably*. Because this isn't an old man's film, it's a young film."
It’s true that Bresson never forgot what if was like to be young and idealistic and searching for meaning. It’s what I love so much about “Four Nights of a Dreamer” too
Yeah, I don't think he ever stopped being idealistic and searching for meaning, even as he saw ever more clearly what a rough time idealism was going to have
